description: our goal is to build an engaging interactive game where players can design, manage, and simulate a space mission, making decisions about mission objectives, spacecraft design, scientific instruments, power, mass, budget, communication, and other mission constraints
summary:
BEYOND ORBIT is a free, retro pixel-art space game that teaches teenagers how a real space mission works, stage by stage.

Players start on a home world (Earth for the Moon mission, the Moon for the Mars mission, following NASA’s Moon to Mars approach). They collect supplies while dodging obstacles, then build a spacecraft from exactly what they found, balancing launch mass, fuel, power, heat protection and budget. After launch, they walk the decks of their ship and face three emergencies, each with 60 seconds to choose between two imperfect solutions, then carry out the repair themselves, sometimes on a tethered spacewalk.

Every emergency is based on real NASA data and resources: live solar-storm data from NASA’s DONKI database, the real Earth–Mars radio delay, real mission history, CubeSat 101, the Mission Design Lab, GMAT and the Webb telescope.

When a mission fails, our Failure Autopsy names the exact mistake, and the Time Machine sends players back to fix it and compare timelines. Beyond Orbit turns failure into learning, and shows young people that space is won by good decisions under pressure
details:
What it does
Beyond Orbit is a 2D side-scrolling space mission game in a classic pixel style, playable in any web browser with no installation. Each mission has four stages:

  1. Collect: explore your home world (Kennedy Space Center on Earth, or Artemis Base Camp on the Moon) and collect supplies while avoiding obstacles such as canals, venting rockets, lightning, alligators, craters, cryo-geysers and meteorite strikes. Oxygen or stamina is limited.
  2. Build: design your spacecraft in a nine-step workshop. Every part costs supplies. Players must keep launch mass, fuel, power, heat protection and budget within limits. Weak choices still let you launch, but they become “technical debt” that causes hazards later.
  3. Fly: inside the spacecraft, three emergencies occur. The player has 60 seconds to reach the right room, choose between two solutions with real pros and cons, and complete a hands-on repair mini-game, sometimes outside the ship on a tethered spacewalk. Emergencies are drawn from a pool, so every new game is different.
  4. Land and review: after landing, players mine rocks for science samples. After a complete success, they walk on the destination, plant their team flag and take photos. The mission report gives a score, a rank and a leaderboard place. A five-expert review board reacts to the mission.

What makes it creative

  • Failure Autopsy: after a failed mission, the game replays the whole flight and names the exact decision or part that caused the failure.
  • Time Machine: players rewind to any past decision, try the other option on a new timeline and compare outcomes side by side.
  • Real consequences: early choices change later events (a “butterfly effect”), so players see cause and effect across a whole system.
  • A retro pixel style that teenagers find familiar, focused on decisions rather than graphics.

Use of NASA data and resources

  • Live coronal mass ejection data from NASA’s DONKI API sets the strength of the Mars radiation storm. A bundled snapshot of real DONKI data is used when offline.
  • The Earth–Mars radio delay is calculated for the current date; on Mars, Mission Control’s advice arrives only after that delay.
  • Every emergency is based on a real event (for example Soyuz MS-22, Galileo, Spirit, STS-120) and shows a card explaining what the real team did.
  • Emergencies and their source cards are built from NASA CubeSat 101, the Mission Design Lab subsystems, GMAT trajectory design, the “Design and Develop Science Missions” segments (launch, space, ground, user), and the Webb “build it yourself” objective → wavelength → instrument approach.

Intended impact
Teenagers learn how a space mission works stage by stage, why engineering is about trade-offs, how to decide under pressure, and that failure is the first step to getting it right. It suits classrooms: one mission fits in a lesson, and a guided Demo mission teaches new players.

Tools and technologies
TypeScript, Phaser 3 (game engine and physics), React 19, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, Vite, Vitest (49 automated tests), the Web Audio API for sound, GitHub and GitHub Actions, and Cloudflare Pages for hosting. All artwork is drawn in code, with no image files. There is no backend: saves and the leaderboard stay in the browser, and no personal data is collected.

Factors we considered
Accessibility (keyboard, gamepad and touch controls, a colour-blind mode, pop-up tutorials, no reflex-heavy requirements), working offline on school Wi-Fi, short play sessions, and no NASA logos or branding (our team flag is our own Koffee Latte design).
